full_text_zh:
[P1] 西游记之五
观潮轩印
紧箍咒

[P2] 紧箍咒
《西游记》之五
原著 吴承恩
改编 卢光照
绘画 盛锡珊
观潮轩印
河北美术出版社

内容提要
唐僧奉圣命去西天取经，路遇狼虫虎豹，蒙猎人刘伯钦相救，后在两界山收了悟空，才得奔往西天。
这段故事是《西游记》中唐僧师徒取经的开始，也是五百年后的孙悟空二次出世的开头。故事表现了唐僧不怕困难的坚强意志，和孙悟空勇敢机智、疾恶如仇的豪侠性格。

[P3] 1 唐僧奉了唐王的命令，带了两个从人，往西天取经。

2 这日，他们来到法门寺，住持僧迎唐僧在寺内安歇。灯下众僧徒议论着往西天路险魔多，恐难通过。唐僧表示一定要到西天，取得经卷。众僧都称赞他的决心。

我曾对佛祖立下誓言，不论多么艰难困苦，一定要到西天，取得经卷。

[P4] 3 第二天早晨，唐僧在寺内用过早斋，两个从人备好了马，三人辞别众僧，又往西行。
4 行走数日，这天来到河州衙，此处是大唐的山河边界。镇边总兵和本处僧众，听说是钦差法师到，都来迎接，当即让唐僧在福原寺安歇。

[P5] 5 唐僧着急赶路，第二天不等天亮，就让从人备好马匹，趁着月光向前行走。刚走十几里路，就入山地，只得拨草寻路。正走间，三人连马跌入坑内。
6 三人正在心慌，忽听得“拿将来！拿将来！”的叫喊声，接着出现了五六十个妖邪，将他们三个揪了上去。

[P6] 7 唐僧偷眼观看，见上面坐着一个魔王，虎头虎脑，十分凶恶。那魔王一声令喝，众小妖将他三人捆绑起来，正要安排吞吃，只听外边喧哗道：‘熊山君、特处士来了。’这魔王慌忙起身迎接。
8 原来来了一个野牛精，一个熊精。两个妖怪向魔王祝贺了一番，魔王就叫左右将两个从人剖腹剜心吞下肚去。

[P7] 9 这时天已发白，众妖怪撇下唐僧，一哄而散。唐僧正吓得昏昏沉沉，忽然一个老翁走向前来，用手一拂，绳索尽断；又对唐僧吹了一口气，唐僧才醒转过来。
10 唐僧正要叩谢老翁，那老翁已跨上一只白鹤腾空而去。唐僧对天仰拜，只见空中飘下一张帖子，上边写的是“太白金星”。唐僧又望空拜了几拜，一个人牵了马匹，孤寂地往前行走。

[P8] 11 唐僧走了好半天，还不见人烟，心中正在烦闷，忽
见前面有三只猛虎咆哮，后面有一条长蛇向他扑来。
12 唐僧自觉这次定难活命了，但忽然又见毒虫爬逃，
恶兽奔走。唐僧抬头看时，只见一个大汉，从山坡上走来。

[P9] 13 唐僧见他走近，跪在路旁，合掌高叫道：“大王救命！”
那人把唐僧扶起道：“我不是大王，我是这里的猎户，名叫
刘伯钦，绰号镇山太保。因为虎狼怕我，所以它们都逃散
了。”
14 唐僧感谢不尽，便把去西天取经的情由告诉了他。
伯钦邀他到家里休息。唐僧满心欢喜，牵了马随他前行。
过了山坡，又听得呼呼风响，伯钦道：“老虎又来了，待我
把它拿住。”

[P10] 15 伯钦说罢，手执钢叉，大踏步迎了上去。那虎见伯钦来了，躲闪不及，索性向伯钦扑来。他两个斗了有一个时辰，那虎渐渐支持不住，被伯钦一叉刺死。
16 伯钦一手执叉，一手拖虎，引唐僧进入山庄。来到家门口，一声呼唤，早有三四个家僮出来，将虎拖进去。伯钦便将唐僧迎入后堂休息。

[P11] 17 第二天，唐僧急要赶路，伯钦送银钱及干粮给唐僧，唐僧坚决不受，说：‘只要你能送我一程，我就心满意足了。’
18 于是，伯钦便带了捕猎器械，陪同唐僧上了大路。行走半日，迎面一座大山，走到半山腰中，伯钦立住道：‘长老，我不能再送了。这山叫两界山，山那边已不属大唐所管。’唐僧苦苦求他再送一程。

[P12] 19 正在这时，只听山脚下喊声如雷：“我师父来也！我师父来也！”这一喊，吓得唐僧心惊胆颤。伯钦说：“长老不要惊慌，这叫声想必是山脚下那石匣中的老猿喊出来的。”
20 唐僧惊问是什么老猿，伯钦道：“曾听老人言讲：古时候，天上忽然降下这座大山，山下压着一个神猴，自古到今，冻饿不死。长老莫怕，我们下山去看个明白。”

[P13] 21 唐僧同伯钦到了山下，只见那石匣中，果然有只猿猴，露着头，向唐僧招手道：‘师父，你怎么这时才来？来得好！来得好！救我出来，我保你上西天取经！’
22 唐僧正要问他，那猴却说：‘我是五百年前大闹天宫的齐天大圣，被如来佛压在这里。观音菩萨说，只要我保你去西天取经，就放我出来。师父，我愿保你去取经，快把我放出来吧！’

[P14] 23 唐僧说：‘只是我没有斧凿，怎么能救你出来？’那猴道：‘不要斧凿，这山顶上有如来佛的一张压帖，将它揭起，我就出来了。’
24 唐僧将信将疑，与伯钦来到山顶上，果然在一块四方大石上贴着一张金光闪烁的帖子。

[P15] 25 唐僧默默祷告一番，然后用手轻轻一揭，只见一阵清风，把压帖儿刮上天空，只听有人喊道：‘我是监押大圣的天神。如今他灾难已满，我回见如来交帖去了！’
26 唐僧连连向空礼拜。拜毕，急下高山，到石匣边，对那猴说：‘押帖揭了，出来吧！’那猴高兴地说：‘好好！师父请走开些，我好出来，莫惊吓着你。’

[P16] 再走！再走！
27 伯钦和唐僧，往山下走去。走了六七里，听得那猴
还高声叫道：‘再走！再走！’伯钦和唐僧，只得再往后退。
28 唐僧和伯钦又走了一程，只听得‘轰隆’一声山崩
地裂的巨响，回头看时，两界山已崩得粉碎。

[P17] 29 唐僧惊慌未定，只见那猴早到了他的跟前，赤裸裸地跪下，说道：‘多谢师父搭救，我出来了。’
30 那猴对唐僧拜了四拜，便起身去给唐僧收拾行李和马匹。

[P18] 31 唐僧见他很有诚心，就收他做了徒弟。问他有无名字，他说叫孙悟空。唐僧又给他起了个混名，称为“行者”，从此他又叫孙行者了。
32 伯钦见唐僧收了个可靠的徒弟，也就放了心。告别唐僧，回往家中。

[P19] 33 孙悟空请唐僧上了马，自己在前边背着行李带路，
正走着，忽然一只猛虎，咆哮着走来。
34 唐僧吓得心惊肉跳，悟空道：‘师父莫怕，它是给我
送衣服来的！’说时迟，那时快，悟空从耳朵里拔出一根针
儿，幌了一幌，变成一根碗来粗的铁棒，飞步上前，一棒
就把那虎打死了。

[P20] 35 唐僧又惊又喜，悟空收了铁棒，说道：‘等我脱下它的衣服来。’说着，拔下一根毫毛，吹了口气，变作一把尖刀，立刻把虎皮剥了下来。
36 悟空把虎皮割成一张方块，用葛藤系在腰间，遮了下体道：‘师父，咱们走吧，等到了人家，再用针缝。’

[P21] 37 师徒二人继续前进，唐僧在马上问道：‘悟空，你刚才打虎的铁棒，怎么不见了？’悟空道：‘我那棒叫如意‘金箍棒’，能大能小，如今变成一根针儿放在耳朵里了。’唐僧听了，惊喜非常。
38 师徒二人走着路，说着话，不知不觉太阳已西坠。悟空催唐僧快走。不多时，来到一座庄院门前。

[P22] 39 唐僧让悟空上前，敲门借宿。门声响处，走出一个老人。老人见悟空那相貌，吓得倒退了几步。唐僧忙道：
“老施主不要怕，他是我的徒弟。”老人见唐僧面貌清秀，
也就不怕了。
40 老人把唐僧和悟空让进家中，做了斋饭招待。饭毕，
悟空又向老人要了热水给唐僧洗浴。

[P23] 41 悟空又向老人借了针线，脱下那幅虎皮，坐在灯下缝起来。悟空觉得自己赤裸裸的不好看，把唐僧脱下的一件白布直裰拿来，披在身上。
42 悟空缝毕，走到唐僧面前道：‘老孙今天这等打扮，比昨日怎样？’唐僧道：‘好！好！这才像个悟空。’又道：‘你不嫌残破，这件直裰儿，就送给你吧！’悟空道了谢，去了。

[P24] 43 第二天一早，悟空备好马匹，唐僧辞别了老人，又向西方前进。
44 师徒二人翻山越岭，正往前行，忽听路旁唿哨一声，闯出六个大汉，手中各持刀枪，拦住去路道：‘你们是哪里的和尚，快留下马匹行李，饶你们性命！’

[P25] 45 唐僧吓得魂不附体。悟空道：‘师父别怕，他是送盘缠来的。’说了，跳向前去，大喝道：‘你们这些毛贼，敢来拦路？快把窃来的财物分给我一半，不然，把你们打个粉碎！’
46 那些大汉听说，立刻怒气冲天，围住悟空，乒乒乓乓，照悟空头上乱砍乱打。悟空站在中间，只当不知。那些贼道：‘好和尚，真个头硬！’

[P26] 47 六个贼人打得手累了，悟空道：‘你们也该看看老孙的厉害了！’说着，从耳朵中拔出一根针儿，迎风一幌，立刻变成一根碗来粗细的铁棒。
48 那些贼吓得乱跑，悟空赶上，一棒一个，统统给打死了。

[P27] 出家人宁死决不敢行凶，似你这样暴横，去不得西天，当不得和尚。
49 悟空夺了他们的银两，笑吟吟地走来对唐僧说：“师父，走吧，那些贼人都被我打死了！”唐僧是个面善心软的人，见杀死了这许多人，不但没夸奖悟空，反而狠狠地把他申斥了一顿。
50 这悟空一生受不得气，见唐僧唠叨不休，早按不住心头的火气，说道：“既然师父说我去不得西天，我何必招你讨厌，那你就自己去西天吧，我老孙去也！”说罢，将身一纵，驾起筋斗云，向东去了。

[P28] 51 唐僧急抬头看时，早不见了悟空。撇下这长老孤孤零零，心中又恨又悔。没奈何，只得独自牵了马匹，向前走去。
52 行不多时，只见山路前面，来了一个婆婆，手里拿着一件绵衣和一顶花帽。唐僧见她走来，便急忙给她让路。

[P29] 53 婆婆问他道：‘你是哪里来的长老，独自一人在这山中行走？’唐僧就把山中遇贼，悟空行凶和不听训教，一气回东方去了的情形说了一遍。那婆婆道：‘不怕，我去叫他回来。’
54 那婆婆又把衣帽送给了唐僧，叫他等悟空回来给他穿戴，还教给了唐僧‘紧箍咒’。那婆婆交代完毕，化作一道金光，向东去了。唐僧情知是观音菩萨传授真言，连忙跪拜。

[P30] 55 再说那悟空，一个筋斗云，转回东洋大海，分开水道，来到水晶宫前。这时早惊动了龙王，忙出来把悟空接到龙宫。
56 宾主坐定，龙王问道：‘听说大圣难满，想必是回来重整花果山复归水帘洞了。’悟空道：‘哪里，我受菩萨劝善，随了东土唐僧往西天取经，当了和尚了。’龙王听了，连连道贺。

[P31] 57 悟空又道：“只是那唐僧不识人性，我打死了几个毛贼他便絮絮叨叨。我老孙一气，撇下他回来了。如今先来望望你，顺便求杯茶吃。”龙王闻言，忙叫龙子龙孙献上茶来。
58 吃完茶，悟空忽然看见墙上挂着一张“圯桥进履”的画儿，问是什么画。龙王说：“这是张良在桥下给仙人黄石公拾鞋的故事。仙人见他有耐性，便把天书传给他，后来他成了汉朝名士。”

[P32] 59 悟空听了，半晌沉思不语。龙王道：‘你不尽心保唐僧取经，怎么能成正果？到头来只不过还是个妖仙。’悟空说：‘要不我还去保他取经？’龙王欣喜道：‘那当然更好。’
60 悟空思想一番，觉得保唐僧去西天取经，才是正理。于是，辞别龙王，驾起云头，又去寻找师父。

[P33] 61 正走间，遇着了观音菩萨。菩萨问他道：‘孙悟空，你不去保唐僧，到这里做什么？’慌得悟空忙施礼道：‘我现在就去。’菩萨道：‘那很好，赶快去，莫错过了时机！’
62 悟空别了菩萨，向西而来。顷刻间看见唐僧正闷闷地坐在路旁。他按下云头，走上前说道：‘师父，怎么不赶路，在这里做什么？’唐僧道：‘你往哪里去了，叫我在此好等。’

[P34] 63 悟空说：‘我到东海龙宫讨了杯茶吃。’唐僧道：‘你只顾自己，我在这里忍饥挨饿，你却不管。’悟空道：‘我去给你化点斋来吃吧！’唐僧道：‘不必，我包袱里还有干粮。’悟空连忙去取。
64 悟空把干粮拿给师父。又见里面有一件绵衣和一顶花帽，悟空心中羡慕，便问道：‘这衣帽是东土带来的么？’唐僧说：‘你若想穿，就送给你吧。’

[P35] 65 悟空高兴地忙戴了帽子，穿了绵衣。唐僧这时不吃干粮，却默默的念那“紧箍咒”刚念一遍，悟空就叫道：“头痛！头痛！
66 唐僧又念了几遍，痛得悟空在地上打滚，不住地乱抓嵌金的花帽。

[P36] 67 唐僧怕他把金箍扯断了，就住口不念了。说来很灵，悟空的头立刻也就不痛了。悟空用手去头上摸摸，似有一条金线，紧紧地勒在头上，取不下，扯不断，好像已经生了根。
68 悟空见师父念咒语治他，不由发怒，取出铁棒，朝唐僧就要下手。慌得唐僧连忙又念起紧箍咒，痛得悟空不住哀求道：‘师父，师父，我以后再也不敢了！’

[P37] 69 悟空问唐僧这法儿是谁教给的，唐僧说是一个婆婆传授的。悟空道：‘定是那南海观音，我去打她去！’唐僧道：‘既然这法是她教我的，当然她更会了，她若念起来，你就活不成了。’
70 悟空一想，觉得有理，只得跪下哀求道：‘我不去找她了，师父你也别念这咒了，我一定好好地保你去西天取经，也得个正果！’唐僧这才放了心，扶起了悟空，安慰了几句，一同往西天取经去了。欲知后事，请看第六册《收白龙马》。

Printed by Guanchao Xuan
Hebei Fine Arts Publishing House

Synopsis
Tang Sanzang, obeying the Buddha's command, sets out for the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures. Along the way, he encounters wolves, insects, tigers, and leopards, and is rescued by the hunter Liu Boqin. Later, at the Mountain of Two Worlds, he recruits Wukong, and finally proceeds toward the Western Heaven.
This story marks the beginning of Tang Sanzang and his disciples' journey to fetch the scriptures in "Journey to the West," and also the start of Sun Wukong's second reincarnation after five hundred years. The story highlights Tang Sanzang's strong will in facing difficulties, and Sun Wukong's brave, intelligent, and righteous character.

[P3] 1 Tang Sanzang, following Emperor Tang's command, brought two attendants to journey westward to fetch scriptures.

2 On this day, they arrived at the Fahmen Temple, where the abbot welcomed Tang Sanzang to rest inside the temple. Under the lamp, the monks discussed how dangerous and full of demons the journey westward was, fearing they might not make it. Tang Sanzang declared his determination to reach the West and obtain the scriptures. All the monks praised his resolve.

I once made a vow to Buddha that no matter how difficult and arduous the journey, I must reach the West and obtain the scriptures.

[P4] 3 The next morning, after having breakfast in the temple, Tang Sanzang's two attendants prepared the horses. The three of them bid farewell to the monks and continued westward.
4 After traveling for several days, they arrived at Hezhou Prefecture, which marked the border of the Great Tang Empire. The local military commander and the monks there, upon hearing that the imperial envoy monk had arrived, came to welcome him. They immediately arranged for Tang Sanzang to rest at Fuyuan Temple.

[P5] 5 Tang Sanzang was in a hurry to travel. The next day, before dawn, he had his attendants ready the horses and proceeded forward under the moonlight. After traveling only十几 li, they entered mountainous terrain and had to clear a path by pulling aside grass. While walking, the three men and their horses fell into a pit.
6 The three were in a state of panic when suddenly they heard the shouts, "Catch them! Catch them!" Soon after, fifty or sixty demons appeared and dragged the three of them up.

[P6] 7 Tang Sanzang glanced secretly and saw a demon king sitting above, with a fierce, tiger-like face. At the demon king's command, the small demons bound the three of them and were about to prepare them for eating, when suddenly a commotion came from outside: 'Bear Mountain Lord, Special Scholar has arrived!' The demon king hurriedly rose to greet them.
8 It turned out that a wild ox spirit and a bear spirit had arrived. The two demons congratulated the demon king, and then the king ordered his attendants to cut open the two servants, remove their hearts, and eat them.

[P7] 9 The sky had already turned pale. The demons left Tang Sanzang and scattered in a hurry. Tang Sanzang, terrified and dazed, suddenly saw an old man approach. With a wave of his hand, the old man broke the ropes; then he blew a breath onto Tang Sanzang, who finally woke up.
10 Just as Tang Sanzang was about to bow to thank the old man, the old man had already mounted a white crane and soared into the sky. Tang Sanzang looked up and bowed to the heavens, only to see a scroll drifting down from the sky, with the words "Taibai Jin Xing" written on it. Tang Sanzang bowed several more times toward the sky, then, alone, led his horse and walked forward in solitude.

[P8] 11 Tang Sanzang had walked for a long time, still seeing no signs of human habitation, and was feeling troubled in his heart, when suddenly he saw three fierce tigers roaring ahead, and a long snake rushing toward him from behind.
12 Tang Sanzang felt certain he would not survive this time, but suddenly he saw the venomous insects crawling away and the ferocious beasts running off. When Tang Sanzang looked up, he saw a big man coming down the hillside.

[P9] 13 Tang Sanzang saw him approaching, knelt by the roadside, and cried out with clasped hands: "Great King, save me!"
That man helped Tang Sanzang up and said: "I am not a king. I am a local hunter named Liu Boqin, nicknamed 'Mountain Guardian'. Because tigers and wolves fear me, they have all scattered."
14 Tang Sanzang thanked him profusely and told him the story of his journey to the West to fetch the scriptures.
Boqin invited him to rest at his home. Tang Sanzang was overjoyed, took his horse, and followed him forward.
After crossing the hill, they heard a roaring wind, and Boqin said: "The tiger is coming again, let me catch it."

[P10] 15 After saying this, Boqin, holding his steel fork, strode forward. The tiger, seeing Boqin coming, couldn't dodge in time and lunged at him. They fought for about an hour, and the tiger gradually weakened, finally being stabbed to death by Boqin's fork.
16 Boqin, holding the fork in one hand and dragging the tiger with the other, led Tang Sanzang into the mountain villa. Upon reaching the front door, he called out, and immediately three or four servants came out to drag the tiger inside. Boqin then welcomed Tang Sanzang into the back hall to rest.

[P11] 17 The next day, Tang Sanzang was eager to continue his journey. Boqin offered him silver and dry rations, but Tang Sanzang firmly refused, saying, 'As long as you can escort me for a while, I will be perfectly content.'
18 So, Boqin brought his hunting gear and accompanied Tang Sanzang on the main road. After walking for half a day, they encountered a large mountain. Halfway up, Boqin stopped and said, 'Master, I can't go any further. This mountain is called Liangjie Mountain, and the other side is no longer under the jurisdiction of the Great Tang.' Tang Sanzang pleaded with him to go just a little further.

[P12] 19 At this moment, a thunderous shout came from the foot of the mountain: "My master is coming! My master is coming!" This shout frightened Master Tang to the core. Boqin said, "Master, don't be alarmed. This cry must be coming from the old ape trapped in the stone box at the foot of the mountain.
20 Master Tang asked in surprise what kind of old ape it was. Boqin replied, "I once heard an old man say: long ago, a great mountain suddenly fell from the sky, pressing down a divine monkey beneath it. Since ancient times, it has neither frozen nor starved to death. Master, don't be afraid. Let's go down the mountain to see for ourselves."

[P13] 21 Tang Sanzang and Boqin arrived at the foot of the mountain. They saw a monkey in the stone box, with his head exposed, waving at Tang Sanzang and saying: 'Master, why are you coming only now? Good timing! Good timing! Rescue me, and I will protect you on your journey to the West to fetch the scriptures!'
22 Just as Tang Sanzang was about to ask him, the monkey said: 'I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, who caused chaos in Heaven five hundred years ago. I was pressed here by Buddha. Guanyin Bodhisattva said that if I protect you on your journey to the West to fetch the scriptures, I will be released. Master, I am willing to protect you on your journey, so quickly release me!'

[P14] 23 Tang Sanzang said: 'I don't have an axe or chisel; how can I rescue you?' The monkey replied: 'No need for an axe or chisel. There is a sealing edict from Buddha on top of this mountain. If you remove it, I will be free.'
24 Tang Sanzang, half-believing and half-doubting, went to the mountain top with Boqin. Indeed, on a large square stone, there was a golden, shimmering edict.

[P15] 25 Tang Sanzang silently prayed for a while, then gently peeled off the seal. A gentle breeze blew, carrying the seal up into the sky. A voice shouted: 'I am the heavenly god who guarded the Great Sage. His tribulations are now complete. I shall return to Buddha to deliver the seal!' 
26 Tang Sanzang bowed repeatedly to the sky. After finishing his bow, he hurried down the mountain to the stone prison, and said to the monkey: 'The seal has been removed. Come out!' The monkey happily replied: 'Alright! Master, please step aside so I can come out. Don't frighten me.'

[P16] Go on! Go on!
27 Boqin and Tang Sanzang walked down the mountain. After walking six or seven li, they heard the monkey shouting loudly: 'Go on! Go on!' Boqin and Tang Sanzang had to retreat again.
28 Tang Sanzang and Boqin walked a bit further, when suddenly they heard a tremendous 'boom'—the sound of mountains collapsing and the earth cracking. Looking back, they saw that the Two Worlds Mountain had shattered into pieces.

[P17] 29 Tang Sanzang was still in shock, when he saw the monkey had already reached his feet, bare and kneeling, saying: 'Thank you, Master, for saving me. I'm out now.'
30 The monkey bowed to Tang Sanzang four times, then got up to pack Tang Sanzang's luggage and saddle the horse.

[P18] 31 Tang Sanzang saw that he was very sincere, so he took him as his disciple. He asked if he had a name, and he said his name was Sun Wukong. Tang Sanzang gave him a nickname, calling him 'Xingzhe', and from then on he was also called Sun Xingzhe.
32 Boqin saw that Tang Sanzang had taken on a reliable disciple, so he felt at ease. He bid farewell to Tang Sanzang and returned home.

[P19] 33 Sun Wukong helped Tang Sanzang onto the horse, carrying the luggage ahead to lead the way. 
As they were walking, suddenly a fierce tiger roared and came toward them. 
34 Tang Sanzang was terrified, trembling with fear. Wukong said: 'Master, don't be afraid, it's here to deliver clothes to me!' Before he could finish, Wukong pulled out a tiny needle from his ear, waved it once, and it transformed into an iron staff as thick as a bowl. He dashed forward and killed the tiger with one blow.

[P20] 35 Tang Sanzang was both surprised and delighted. Wukong put away his iron staff and said, 'Let me take off its clothes.' Saying that, he plucked a single hair, blew on it, and it turned into a sharp knife. He immediately skinned the tiger.
36 Wukong cut the tiger skin into a square piece, tied it around his waist with a vine to cover his lower body, and said, 'Master, let's go. We'll sew it up when we reach a house.'

[P21] 37 The master and disciple continued forward. Tang僧 asked from his horse, 'Wukong, where is the iron staff you used to kill the tiger?' Wukong replied, 'My staff is called the Ruyi Jingu Bang. It can grow big or small. Now it has become a tiny needle stored in my ear.' Tang僧 listened and was greatly delighted.
38 The master and disciple walked and talked, and before they knew it, the sun had already set. Wukong urged Tang僧 to hurry. Soon, they arrived at the gate of a farmhouse.

[P22] 39 The monk told Wukong to go forward and knock on the door to ask for lodging. When the door opened, an old man came out. Seeing Wukong's appearance, the old man was frightened and stepped back a few paces. The monk hurriedly said: 
"Old master, don't be afraid, he is my disciple." Seeing the monk's handsome face, the old man was no longer afraid.
40 The old man invited the monk and Wukong into his home, prepared vegetarian food to entertain them. After the meal, 
Wukong asked the old man for hot water to bathe the monk.

[P23] 41 Wukong borrowed needles and thread from the old man, took off the tiger skin, and sat under the lamp to sew it. Wukong felt that he looked bare and unattractive, so he took the white cloth robe that Tang Sanzang had taken off and draped it over himself.
42 After finishing sewing, Wukong walked up to Tang Sanzang and said, 'Old Master, how does this outfit look today compared to yesterday?' Tang Sanzang replied, 'Good! Good! This looks more like Wukong.' He then added, 'If you don't mind its worn condition, I'll give you this robe!' Wukong thanked him and left.

[P24] 43 The next morning, Wukong prepared the horse, and Tang Sanzang bid farewell to the old man, then continued westward.
44 The master and disciple were crossing mountains and ridges, moving forward, when suddenly they heard a whistle from the roadside. Six big men burst out, each holding a knife or spear, blocking their path and shouting: 'You monks, where are you from? Quickly leave your horse and luggage, and we'll spare your lives!'

[P25] 45 Tang Sanzang was terrified, his soul seeming to leave his body. Wukong said, 'Master, don't be afraid, he's here to deliver the travel money.' Then, he leapt forward and shouted, 'You bandits, dare to block our path? Hand over half of the stolen goods, or I'll beat you to pieces!'
46 Upon hearing this, the men became furious, surrounded Wukong, and hacked at him wildly with clashing weapons. Wukong stood in the middle, pretending not to notice. The bandits shouted, 'Good monk, your head is truly hard!'

[P26] 47 The six bandits were tired from fighting. Wukong said, 'You should see how powerful I am!' Saying that, he pulled out a needle from his ear, waved it in the wind, and it instantly turned into an iron rod as thick as a bowl.
48 The bandits, frightened, ran wildly. Wukong chased after them, striking one with each blow, and killed them all.

[P27] Monks would rather die than commit violence; with such brutality, you cannot reach the Western Heaven, nor become a monk.
49 Wukong took their silver, walked over smiling to Tang Sanzang and said, "Master, let's go—the bandits are all dead!" Tang Sanzang, being kind-hearted, saw that so many people had been killed, and instead of praising Wukong, scolded him harshly.
50 Wukong, who could never bear to be insulted, saw Tang Sanzang nagging endlessly and could no longer hold back his anger. He said, "Since you say I cannot reach the Western Heaven, why should I make you dislike me? Then go to the Western Heaven yourself—I, Old Sun, am leaving!" Saying this, he leaped up, mounted the Cloud of Somersault, and flew eastward.

[P28] 51 Tang Sanzang hurriedly looked up, but Wukong was already gone. Left alone, the elder felt both angry and regretful. With no choice, he had to lead his horse forward alone.
52 After walking a short while, he saw an old woman coming down the mountain path, holding a woolen coat and a floral hat. Tang Sanzang saw her approaching and quickly made way for her.

[P29] 53 The old woman asked him, 'Where are you from, elder, traveling alone in these mountains?' Tang Sanzang recounted how he encountered bandits, how Wukong acted violently and disobeyed instructions, and how he had stormed back east in anger. The old woman said, 'Don't worry, I'll go call him back.'
54 The old woman then gave Tang Sanzang clothes and a hat, telling him to wait for Wukong to return and wear them, and also taught him the 'Tightening Spell'. After finishing her instructions, the old woman transformed into a beam of golden light and went east. Tang Sanzang realized it was Guanyin Bodhisattva imparting the true words, and immediately knelt to pay his respects.

[P30] 55 Then, Wukong, with a single somersault cloud, returned to the Eastern Sea, parted the waters, and arrived at the Crystal Palace. The Dragon King had already been alerted and hurried out to welcome Wukong into the palace.
56 After they were seated, the Dragon King asked, 'I heard your tribulations have ended. Surely you've returned to restore Flower-Fruit Mountain and return to Water Curtain Cave.' Wukong replied, 'No, I've been persuaded by the Bodhisattva to do good, and I've followed the monk from the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. I've become a monk now.' The Dragon King, upon hearing this, congratulated him repeatedly.

[P31] 57 Wukong said, “It’s just that Master Tang doesn’t understand human nature. I killed a few bandits, and he kept nagging. I got so angry, I left him behind. I’ve come to visit you first, and I’d like to have a cup of tea.” Hearing this, the Dragon King hurriedly called his dragon sons and grandsons to serve tea.
58 After finishing the tea, Wukong suddenly saw a painting hanging on the wall titled “The Bridge of the Lost Shoe.” He asked what it was. The Dragon King said, “This is the story of Zhang Liang picking up the shoe for the immortal Huang Shigong under the bridge. The immortal, seeing his patience, gave him the Heavenly Book, and later he became a famous minister of the Han dynasty.”

[P32] 59 Wukong listened and remained silent for a while, deep in thought. The Dragon King said, 'If you don't wholeheartedly protect Tang Sanzang on his journey to fetch the scriptures, how can you achieve enlightenment? In the end, you'll just remain a demon spirit.' Wukong replied, 'Then perhaps I should go back and protect him on his journey?' The Dragon King happily responded, 'That would be even better.'
60 After thinking it over, Wukong realized that protecting Tang Sanzang on his journey to the West to fetch the scriptures was the right path. So, he bid farewell to the Dragon King, mounted the clouds, and set off once more to find his master.

[P33] 61 While walking, he met Guanyin Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva asked him, 'Sun Wukong, why aren't you protecting Tang Sanzang? What are you doing here?' Startled, Wukong hurriedly bowed and said, 'I'll go right away.' The Bodhisattva said, 'That's good, hurry up, don't miss the opportunity!'
62 Wukong bid farewell to the Bodhisattva and headed west. In a moment, he saw Master Tang sitting dejectedly by the roadside. He descended from the clouds, approached, and said, 'Master, why aren't you continuing your journey? What are you doing here?' Tang Sanzang replied, 'Where did you go? I've been waiting for you here.'

[P34] 63 Wukong said, 'I went to the Dragon King's palace in the East Sea and had a cup of tea.' Tang Sanzang replied, 'You only think of yourself. I'm starving here, and you don't care.' Wukong said, 'I'll go get you some food!' Tang Sanzang said, 'No need, I still have dry rations in my pack.' Wukong hurried to get them.
64 Wukong brought the dry rations to his master. He then saw a warm coat and a floral hat inside, and felt envious. He asked, 'Did you bring these clothes from the Eastern Land?' Tang Sanzang said, 'If you want to wear them, I'll give them to you.'

[P35] 65 Wukong happily put on the hat and wore the warm coat. At this moment, Tang僧 didn't eat the dry food, but silently chanted the 'Tightening Spell'. After just one chant, Wukong cried out: "Headache! Headache!"
66 Tang僧 chanted it a few more times, causing Wukong to roll on the ground in pain, frantically grabbing his golden-embellished flower hat.

[P36] 67 The monk feared he might break the golden hoop, so he stopped reciting the spell. Amazingly, Wukong's head instantly stopped hurting. Wukong touched his head and felt what seemed like a golden thread tightly bound around it—unable to be removed or pulled off, as if it had taken root.
68 Wukong, seeing his master use the spell against him, became furious, pulled out his iron staff, and was about to strike the monk. The monk, frightened, quickly recited the Tightening Hoop spell again. In agony, Wukong kept pleading: 'Master, master, I'll never do it again!'

[P37] 69 Wukong asked Tang僧 who taught him this method. Tang僧 said it was taught by an old woman. Wukong said: 'It must be that Guanyin of the South Sea; I'll go beat her up!' Tang僧 said: 'Since she taught me this method, of course she knows it better. If she recites it, you won't survive.'
70 Wukong thought for a moment and found it reasonable. He knelt down and pleaded: 'I won't go look for her anymore. Master, please don't recite the spell. I will surely protect you on your journey to the West to fetch the scriptures and attain enlightenment!' Tang僧 finally felt at ease, lifted Wukong up, comforted him a few words, and together they continued their journey to the West to fetch the scriptures. To learn what happens next, please read the sixth volume, 'Capturing the White Dragon Horse.'

full_summary_zh:
[P1] 本页为《西游记》第五册的封面，画面描绘了孙悟空被紧箍咒折磨的场景，下方标题为“紧箍咒”，并有“观潮轩印”和“西游记之五”的印章。
[P2] 本页为《西游记》第五册的扉页，包含书名、作者、改编者、绘画者、出版社信息及内容提要，概述了唐僧取经初期收服孙悟空的故事情节。
[P3] 本页描绘了唐僧奉命西天取经，途经法门寺时，住持僧迎其入寺安歇，众僧议论西行艰险，唐僧坚定表示必取经卷，获得众僧称赞。
[P4] 唐僧在法门寺用过早斋后，与随从辞别众僧，继续西行。数日后抵达河州衙，受到镇边总兵和当地僧众的迎接，并被安排在福原寺安歇。
[P5] 唐僧师徒在月夜赶路时，因山路难行跌入坑中，随后被五六十个妖邪发现并捉走。
[P6] 唐僧师徒被妖怪捉住后，被魔王囚禁并准备吃掉。此时，野牛精和熊精前来拜访，魔王为招待他们，下令将两名随从剖腹剜心吃掉。
[P7] 唐僧被妖怪囚禁后，一位老翁现身救下他并使其苏醒。老翁离去时化作白鹤飞走，空中飘下写有“太白金星”的帖子，唐僧拜谢后独自牵马前行。
[P8] 唐僧在荒山中行走，遭遇三只猛虎和一条长蛇的围攻，危在旦夕；正当他绝望时，毒虫和恶兽突然逃走，一个大汉从山坡上走来。
[P9] 唐僧在荒山中被猛虎围困，危急时被猎户刘伯钦救下。唐僧向刘伯钦说明西行取经的来由，刘伯钦邀请他到家中休息，二人一同前行，途中又遇老虎，刘伯钦准备将其擒获。
[P10] 猎户刘伯钦与老虎搏斗并将其刺死，随后带着唐僧回到山庄，让家僮拖走老虎，并将唐僧迎入后堂休息。
[P11] 第二天，猎户刘伯钦欲送银钱干粮给唐僧，唐僧婉拒，只愿他送一程。随后二人同行至两界山，伯钦因山界已出大唐疆域而停步，唐僧恳求再送一程。
[P12] 唐僧与猎户刘伯钦在两界山听到山下传来“我师父来也”的巨响，唐僧惊恐，刘伯钦解释可能是被压在石匣中的老猿所喊，并决定下山查看。
[P13] 唐僧与刘伯钦来到两界山下，发现被压在石匣中的孙悟空。孙悟空向唐僧招手，请求他救自己出来，并承诺保护他西天取经。
[P14] 唐僧与刘伯钦在两界山山顶找到孙悟空所说的如来佛压帖，准备揭帖救出被压的孙悟空。
[P15] 唐僧在两界山山顶揭下如来佛的压帖，压帖被清风卷走，天神宣告孙悟空的灾难已满；随后唐僧下山，对石匣中的孙悟空说押帖已揭，孙悟空高兴地请他走开以便自己出来。
[P16] 唐僧与刘伯钦下山后，孙悟空不断催促他们前行，二人被迫后退；随后，两界山突然崩裂粉碎，二人回头目睹了这一景象。
[P17] 孙悟空被救出后，向唐僧跪拜致谢，并起身为其收拾行李和马匹。
[P18] 唐僧收孙悟空为徒，并赐其混名“行者”，猎户刘伯钦见状放心，告别唐僧返回家中。
[P19] 孙悟空背着行李为唐僧带路，途中遇到猛虎，他用金箍棒一棒将其打死，保护了师父。
[P20] 孙悟空打死猛虎后，用毫毛变出尖刀剥下虎皮，并将其割成方块系在腰间遮体，随后劝唐僧继续赶路。
[P21] 唐僧与孙悟空继续前行，唐僧询问金箍棒去向，孙悟空解释其能大能小并藏于耳中；随后二人边走边谈，不知不觉太阳西落，来到一座庄院门前。
[P22] 唐僧与孙悟空来到一座庄院前借宿，孙悟空敲门后，老人因他相貌吓退，唐僧解释后老人安心；老人招待二人用斋，饭后孙悟空又为唐僧要热水洗浴。
[P23] 孙悟空用虎皮缝制衣物，并披上唐僧的白布直裰遮体；缝好后向唐僧展示，唐僧称赞并把直裰送给他，孙悟空道谢后离开。
[P24] 第二天一早，唐僧与孙悟空辞别老人后继续西行，途中遭遇六个持刀枪的强盗拦路抢劫，要求他们交出马匹和行李。
[P25] 唐僧与孙悟空遭遇六个强盗拦路抢劫，孙悟空声称强盗是来送盘缠的，并威胁分赃，强盗们愤怒围攻，用刀枪乱砍孙悟空，但孙悟空毫不在意，强盗们惊叹其头颅坚硬。
[P26] 孙悟空在与六个强盗的打斗中，因对方打累了，便从耳中取出金箍棒，将其变大，随后追上逃跑的强盗，一棒一个将他们全部打死。
[P27] 孙悟空杀死强盗后向唐僧报信，唐僧因他杀生而责骂他；孙悟空受不住责备，一气之下驾云向东离去。
[P28] 孙悟空离开后，唐僧独自牵马前行，途中遇见一位手持绵衣和花帽的老妇人，唐僧急忙为她让路。
[P29] 唐僧向一位老妇人诉说了孙悟空因杀强盗被责骂后离去的事，老妇人表示会叫他回来。随后，老妇人将衣帽送给唐僧，并传授了‘紧箍咒’，之后化作金光离去，唐僧认出是观音菩萨，连忙跪拜。
[P30] 孙悟空回到东海龙宫，龙王迎接他并询问其近况，孙悟空告知自己受菩萨劝善，已随唐僧西天取经，龙王听后连连道贺。
[P31] 孙悟空回到东海龙宫，向龙王抱怨唐僧因他杀强盗而责骂他，于是负气离开。龙王请他喝茶，孙悟空在喝茶时看到墙上‘圯桥进履’的画，龙王向他讲述了张良拾鞋得天书的故事。
[P32] 孙悟空在龙王的劝说下，反思自己行为，决定返回保护唐僧西天取经，并辞别龙王驾云去找师父。
[P33] 孙悟空在返回途中遇到观音菩萨，菩萨劝他赶快回去保护唐僧。随后，孙悟空找到正在路边等候的唐僧，向他道歉并重新归队。
[P34] 孙悟空回到唐僧身边，为师父取来干粮，并对唐僧包袱里的绵衣和花帽表示羡慕，唐僧便将衣帽赠予他。
[P35] 孙悟空戴上唐僧赠予的帽子和绵衣后，唐僧默念紧箍咒，孙悟空随即头痛难忍，唐僧继续念咒，孙悟空在地上打滚，痛苦地抓挠帽子。
[P36] 唐僧停止念紧箍咒后，孙悟空头痛消失，发现金箍已牢牢勒在头上；当唐僧再次念咒时，孙悟空愤怒欲动手，但因疼痛而哀求认错。
[P37] 孙悟空因不满紧箍咒而欲找观音算账，唐僧劝阻并说明咒语由观音所授。孙悟空最终认错，跪地哀求唐僧不再念咒，并承诺好好保护师父西天取经，二人和好如初，继续踏上取经之路。
